title: Which “is” should training score?

beats.say: The owner asks, “How is my dog?” The sitter replies, “She is happy.” Look at the two copies of “is.” Both have token ID one hundred two in our toy vocabulary. Which prediction should count when we train the assistant to answer?

The one in the reply. Keep its token ID as the label. Under the user’s “is,” put minus one hundred. That tells the loss to skip this prediction. The model still reads the whole question when it predicts the reply.

After “happy” comes the end-of-turn marker. Keep its label too. Count the four marks under She, is, happy, and the ending. Together they teach the sitter’s reply and where to hand the conversation back.

title: What answer does the policy support?

beats.say: An engineer asks about an eighteen-day-old service key. Compare the dot with the cutoff in policy P fourteen. Keys older than fourteen days need a rotation ticket before further use. Exactly fourteen days is on the boundary. Eighteen is past it. What should the approved reply ask the engineer to open?

A rotation ticket. Look at the first word of the approved reply, Open. A base model already predicts the next token from everything before it. A demonstration teaches it which continuation we want in the assistant turn. Suppose it gives Open a one-in-four chance and puts the rest on one other choice. Supervised fine-tuning minimizes the negative log probability of the selected words.

For one word, the gradient on each logit is its probability minus its target. Open gets a target of one. A descent step raises its logit and lowers the other one. With shared weights, updates for different words can pull in different directions.
Now accept the answer “No ticket required.” The loss rewards that answer, even though it contradicts the policy in the request. Here the application supplies the policy in the system message.

Keep retrieved text and tool results in their own roles so you can trace each claim to its source. The row also teaches an ending. At serving time the decoder needs the matching stop ID and a budget for the reply.

title: What did the demonstrations teach?

beats.say: What counts as a good answer during training? InstructGPT first learned from demonstrations. People then ranked answers, a reward model learned those preferences, and P P O used its scores. F L A N learned from instruction-formatted tasks. Its researchers tested whether the model could follow instructions on task types held out of fine-tuning.

Each square stands for one demonstration. LIMA fine-tuned a sixty-five-billion-parameter LLaMA on one thousand curated demonstrations without reinforcement learning. The authors called their explanation the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis. They proposed that pretraining had already taught much of the capability, and the examples helped the model express it. Fine-tuning can also teach new facts and skills.

Suppose a narrow adaptation improves policy answers while lowering a coding score. Keep the tokenizer, template, decoding and evaluation cases fixed, and repeat the comparison. A reproducible loss of earlier capability may be forgetting. Then compare smaller update budgets, broader approved instruction data or replay. Record the sampling probabilities and loss weights.
InstructGPT’s pre-training-gradient mixture was in its reinforcement-learning stage. For your supervised run, compare replay mixtures on the same held-out tasks.

title: The template turns messages into one stream

beats.say: Begin with an ordinary exchange. The user asks, How is my dog? The assistant answers, She is happy. The user follows with, Why? The assistant replies, She is playing. A chat template adds role and turn markers around those familiar words.

Read across the splice. Each position carries one token ID. Here the role header opens the turn, and each reply has an ending. Other model families use different delimiters. Even whitespace can change the IDs. Inspect the tail separately for a known answer, a fresh request, and an unfinished assistant message.

title: Where does the assistant start writing?

beats.say: Start with the same policy and question in all three rows. This small ChatML example changes only what comes next. Training writes the assistant’s known answer and closes its turn. Fresh generation writes the assistant header and waits for an answer. Assistant prefill writes the start of an answer and leaves that message open.
Predict what happens if a request asks both to start a new assistant message and to continue the final one.

Those intents conflict, so the serializer rejects the combination. In this toy a prefill must end in an assistant role. Transformers can continue a final message more generally, including a named reasoning field when its template supports it.

Look at the open JSON field. The model can continue right there. When it finishes, parse the JSON, check the fields and compare the values with the policy. A text-generation pipeline may treat a final assistant message as a prefill by default. Choose the mode explicitly.
For a hosted endpoint, check whether its request format supports prefills.

title: Count the actual pinned tokenizer output

beats.say: Now replace the toy serializer with the public tokenizer for Mistral seven B Instruct version zero point one, pinned to the article’s revision. No model weights are loaded.
Its system text and user question form a forty-four-ID prefix, with two newlines between the fields inside one instruction block. There is no separate assistant header in this template.

The known answer Open a rotation ticket before further use adds eight IDs and E O S, producing fifty-three IDs. The open JSON prefill adds eight IDs without E O S, producing fifty-two. Fresh generation remains forty-four: the generation flag adds nothing to this pinned template.
The model starts its response after the closing instruction delimiter.

One-step template tokenization equals rendering followed by tokenization with added special tokens disabled. Enabling them again duplicates the beginning token: two instead of one. Marker atomicity comes from the vocabulary and encoding settings.

A dot on these enlarged pieces represents a leading space. Here the visible opening instruction marker uses three IDs and its closing marker uses four. Other checkpoints have different boundaries and supported role schemas.

title: Who supplied these five characters?

beats.say: A manual quotes the five characters on the left. The template uses the same spelling to end a turn. Our toy encoder knows who supplied each piece. It assigns the template ending a single control ID, two.
For quoted text it assigns one ordinary ID to each character. You can read the same five characters on screen and send very different IDs to the model.

Now look at the two matches in the pinned tokenizer inspection. Four ordinary vocabulary pieces match in each place. A manual inside the user message owns the first match. The template owns the second. What information would let the application tell those occurrences apart?
Keep each message span and its source. A checker can flag an unexpected occurrence inside the user span for review. The matching IDs tell us what was encoded. The span tells us who supplied it.

The same problem arises if a manual quotes a reserved ending. For this checkpoint that spelling can become an end ID. If we split special spellings across the whole transcript, we change the genuine template ending as well. Both need an ownership check.
Apply the input policy to the user content and verify the serialized result.

title: What did the tokenizer check establish?

beats.say: The article reports a translation study from November twenty twenty-six on one quantized Mistral build on Apple hardware. In all three conditions, the model received a sentence to translate and the same competing request for a fixed-word reply. Each grid has five rows of five dots. Five sentences times five trials gives twenty-five replies per condition.

The investigators ignored case and stripped spaces and periods from both ends of each reply. They counted a match only when the whole reply then matched the test word. The plain-text condition gave zero matches. The marker condition gave twenty-four. The third condition, which also included an ending, gave twenty-five. Each dot represents one recorded reply. These counts describe this build, these requests and this scoring rule. A different deployment needs its own measurements.

There are three different observations here. You can inspect the text the template rendered. You can count the matching IDs and check which message owns them. To learn how the assistant responds, you need a behavioral evaluation on the deployed path.
A defensive input policy can flag or rewrite risky content before rendering. Measure the remaining behavior on held-out requests.

If a hosted service hides the token stream, inspect what you can see. Compare the request bodies and reported input counts. Extra tools, repeated turns or a missing tool result can change them. Include benign quoted markers in your behavioral checks, and restrict access to traces that contain user text or secrets.

title: An internal space survives trimming the outside

beats.say: On the strip, a backslash followed by n stands for a newline. The article’s loose Jinja template places three spaces inside the stream, directly before the end marker, plus outer newlines. Its exact counterpart places no such gap. Trimming only the outside leaves those internal spaces untouched. Whitespace controls should produce the checkpoint’s intended bytes, including any spaces or newlines it requires.

Compare bytes and token IDs separately. In the first toy case an internal space changes the bytes. A normalizer collapses it, so the IDs match. In the second case both renderers produce the same bytes, but the second tokenization adds a beginning ID. A digest identifies the resolved template, while a filename can survive either edit.

Keep golden single-turn, multi-turn, Unicode, code-indentation, quoted-marker and supported empty-content cases, plus an open assistant prefill. Pin checkpoint and tokenizer revisions, resolved template digest, special-token settings and truncation policy. Freeze any clock input in a template-driven test. Unknown differences block the parity decision until explained.

title: Reject incomplete demonstrations before serialization

beats.say: This lab’s completed text-only S F T row permits an optional initial system turn, then alternating user and assistant messages, ending with an assistant answer. That contract rejects empty and system-only rows, a user with no answer, two consecutive user messages, and a system message inserted midway. It accepts several complete user-assistant exchanges.

A fresh generation request instead ends with a completed user turn, because the answer is not yet known. Validate against the intended mode. Tool interactions, multimodal records and assistant-only completion datasets need their own schemas; do not force them through this lab’s alternating text validator.

Read row zero-zero-five. Its messages follow the required role order. Policy P fourteen requires a rotation ticket before further use when a key is older than fourteen days. The answer says that even after fourteen days, no rotation ticket is required. It reverses the rule. A role label records message structure. Check the source of the message and the support for its answer separately.

title: Generate variations and preserve the review boundary

beats.say: Hand review can check a policy version directly but costs time and can miss cases. Self-Instruct began with one hundred seventy-five human seed tasks, generated instructions and instances, and filtered invalid or similar material. Its historical similarity screen used a ROUGE L threshold of zero point seven.
That screen removes near duplicates. Checking the answer against the policy takes a separate review.

Evol-Instruct varies a task’s constraints, depth or breadth. Take a key exactly fourteen days old. The age clause applies only above fourteen, so this key is at the boundary. UltraChat simulates multi-turn conversations. A follow-up introduces a second key, eighteen days old. Look at its age on the same scale. What does the clause require now? That key needs a rotation ticket before further use. A generator can vary the question and still carry a mistaken answer into many rows.

For generated code, use an isolated runner and meaningful tests. Record which cases pass, fail, time out or give different results across runs. If reviewers and a model judge disagree, check the answer against the source. Version evidence snapshots, generator prompts, gates, decisions and accepted data together.

title: Check a negated answer against its source

beats.say: Return to policy P fourteen. The lexical screen requires fourteen days and rotation ticket, and rejects thirty days. Row zero-zero-five says that even after fourteen days no rotation ticket is required. Predict the lexical decision before consulting the source review.
It contains both required strings and no forbidden string, so the screen passes it.

Look at the word “no.” The policy requires a ticket. The candidate says the opposite, so the reviewer rejects it. Row zero-zero-two fails the lexical screen, while zero-zero-one, zero-zero-three and zero-zero-four survive both gates. A faithful paraphrase can miss a required keyword too.

The three accepted rows contain two stale-key cases and one temporary-admin-approval case under the separate policy P seven. They contain zero source-citation cases. Another copy of a stale-key answer would still leave the citation example missing. Keep held-out evaluation cases separate from these training exercises.

title: Which position predicts the next token?

beats.say: Back to the dog. Look at the first She, at position six. The model has to guess that word using only what came before it. Which position made the prediction we should score?
Position five, the assistant header. The model has read the whole question by then. Six is where we find the word that tells us how good the guess was. That one-place gap is the causal shift.

Now She predicts is. Move one place and is predicts happy. One more and happy predicts the turn ending. In each pair, look at the word on the right to decide whether we want that prediction in the loss.

If your model shifts internally, give it labels aligned with the input IDs. When you call raw cross-entropy yourself, pair each logit with the following label. Applying both shifts would pair a logit with the token two positions ahead. Check the first pair again after truncation.

title: What does the model read, and what gets scored?

beats.say: Send all seventeen tokens through the model. Both questions go in, both replies go in, and so do the markers between them. Under each token, start with a copy of its ID. We can now choose which predictions to score.

On the label track, skip the words in the questions. Skip the role headers too. Minus one hundred tells the loss to ignore those positions. Keep the words in both replies and their ending markers. That gives us four targets in each reply, eight altogether. This is our assistant-only loss mask.
Find the second She. Its label is active. Can the model still use the user’s Why to predict that word?
Yes. Trace She back to its assistant header, then follow the input all the way back to the first user turn. Why is in that prefix, even though predicting Why earns no loss term. Look at the word is.
It has the same ID in the first question and in both replies. The template tells us which message owns each copy. Use those token boundaries when you build the labels.

title: What goes into the mean loss?

beats.say: Keep the eight targets we just marked. For each one, take minus the natural logarithm of the probability the model assigned to the token that actually came next. A confident correct guess costs less. Add the eight losses and divide by eight. An ignored label adds nothing to either part of that fraction.

Change just the objective. Score the whole transcript and we get sixteen targets. There are still seventeen inputs. The very first token has no earlier predictor in this row. This choice can train a model to predict user text too.
Studies have found benefits in some long-prompt, short-answer and small-data settings. Compare the objectives on held-out conversations for your task.

Now suppose a bad mask ignores every target. The denominator falls to zero. Reject that row before taking the mean. If an entire batch has zero targets, it has no defined mean loss. In a good row, prompt representations can still affect the reply through attention and shared weights, even when their own labels are ignored.

title: Find the first scored prediction in the real row

beats.say: Here is the end of the real Mistral training row. In this template the closing bracket finishes the user block. Open starts the reply. In the documented TRL training path, the assistant-only setting needs the resolved template to mark the generation span.
Some families have a patched training template. For this checkpoint we mark the existing assistant branch, including its ending. The rendered text and token IDs stay the same.

Inspect the mask that tokenization returns. It selects eight answer pieces and the ending, nine targets altogether. Everything through position forty-three has an ignored label. Look at Open in the label row. Which position predicts it?

Position forty-three predicts Open. The bracket itself has an ignored label, but its logit can still be scored against the next token. At the other end, the period at fifty-one predicts the ending. Fifty-two is a target, and its own final logit has nothing left to predict.

Back in a conversation with two replies, both annotated answers can receive loss. If you want the earlier reply only as context, put the history in the prompt and the last answer in the completion. Select assistant tokens inside that completion.
The earlier reply is still available when the model predicts the later one. Check which ending the resolved annotation actually includes.

title: What did it cost to predict “Open ticket”?

beats.say: Let’s do the arithmetic with six toy symbols. The user asks a question, the assistant replies Open ticket, and the row ends. In the unshifted labels, keep Open, ticket, and end. Here we call cross-entropy directly, so pair each logit with the next label ourselves.
A model that does this internally needs the original unshifted labels.

Suppose the header gives Open a probability of one half. Then Open gives ticket one quarter. Finally ticket gives the ending four fifths. The longest bar belongs to ticket, the least likely of the three observed targets.

Add the three negative natural logarithms before rounding. Their sum is about two point three nats. Divide by three and the mean is about point seven seven nats per scored target. Only the scored targets enter that denominator.

Run the backward pass on those supplied logits. Three rows receive a direct gradient. They belong to the header, Open and ticket. The header gets a gradient because it predicts Open. Skip the shift and follow the vertical arrow under Open. That logit already sees Open in its input and gets scored for copying it.

Shift twice. Follow the arrow from the question at position one. It now predicts Open at three. The assistant header at two skips over Open and predicts ticket at four. Open at three predicts the ending at five. All three targets still count, but each has the wrong predictor. Checking the pairs catches an error that counting targets misses. We can check this with toy logits before training.

title: Three fives at the end of a row

beats.say: Keep the little reply, Open ticket, and its ending. Give this row two padding slots. Here the ending and both pads have the same ID, five. Try the rule that erases every five. The answer words still have targets. Look what happened to the end.

Here are the flags saved during collation. The valid span ends just after the real ending. The reply span starts at Open and ends at that same edge. A one means the position is inside. Use both rows. Which of the three fives belongs in the loss?

Keep the first five, right after ticket. Both flags are one there. The model now practices predicting an ending after ticket. The two padding positions stay ignored. Carry those flags through truncation too, then check that the real ending survived.

title: A row can keep answers while losing its ending

beats.say: Carry token IDs, validity, assistant membership and message ownership through the same truncation. Cutting before every assistant target leaves zero supervised targets. Cutting after answer words but before their genuine ending leaves a positive count yet loses the chosen stop target. Check both properties after truncation, not just before.

An answer can also survive while its policy evidence is removed. A fluent target then practices answering without the intended grounding context. Prefer deliberate whole-message decisions that protect application instructions and required evidence; check references such as that one and complete tool values.
A context that fits visually on a page need not fit the model.

Count the final serialized prompt, including role markers, retrieved passages, tools and any prefill. Add the reserved generated answer and API overhead. In the reader example, seven thousand nine hundred input tokens plus five hundred reserved output tokens exceed an eight-thousand-one-hundred-ninety-two-token limit by two hundred eight.
Whole-message removal may need to cut more than that lower bound.

title: Packing uses more of the token window

beats.say: Short conversations leave empty slots in a fixed window. Our four conversations have nine, six, seven and five tokens. Each window holds sixteen. Separate padding allocates sixty-four slots for twenty-seven tokens. Can the same four conversations fit into two windows?

Visit the rows in input order. Put each row into the first window with room. Nine goes in the first window. Six fits beside it. Seven needs a second window. Five joins seven there. Count the used slots in each window.
Occupied slots rise from about 42 percent to about 84 percent. The same twenty-seven tokens now fit in two windows. To measure speed, time a training step.

Try a second pack with sixteen slots per window. The ten-token row occupies window one, and the eight-token row occupies window two. Six tokens arrive next. They fit in either window. Which one does first fit choose?

Place the six beside the ten. First fit starts its search at window one for every row. That leaves sixteen occupied slots in the first window and eight in the second. Putting the six beside the eight would use the same total space and give a different placement. Inspect the rows as well as the occupancy.

title: What can a packed reply read?

beats.say: The first-fit example measures occupied slots. Real packing strategies make additional data decisions. In the documented TRL path, best-fit decreasing drops overflow beyond the maximum length. Its split variant chunks long examples before packing. Wrapped packing concatenates a raw stream and cuts fixed blocks. These choices can change which context a retained answer sees.

Conversation A ends after three tokens. Conversation B gets the next three. In a variable-length attention call, the cumulative sequence lengths are zero, three and six. The kernel uses those boundaries to keep each conversation’s history separate. Some Transformer paths construct the boundaries from position resets.
Check that your collator passes the boundaries your kernel uses.

Watch the middle token in B. In this CPU attention check, true means a key is visible. With dropout off and equal scores, that token averages ten and twenty to get fifteen. Add a thousand to each value in A. What happens to B’s average?

It stays fifteen. B can still read just ten and twenty. Try the same change through your trainer to check that its attention kernel keeps the conversations separate. Then check the shifted label where the two conversations meet.

title: The attention mask defines who can read whom

beats.say: Causal attention already blocks future tokens. Independent packed conversations need one more restriction: a token in conversation B cannot read conversation A. The allowed matrix is block diagonal, with each conversation's own causal triangle inside its block.

With equal attention scores, ordinary causal attention at B's middle token averages values one, two, three, ten, and twenty. The result is 7.2. An isolated mask admits only B's ten and twenty, producing 15 and removing A from B's computation.

title: Mask the target at every packed boundary

beats.say: Isolated attention does not finish the packing contract. A global one-token shift makes the last logit from A predict the first token in B. If the conversations are independent, that boundary target must be ignored as well.

Change every value in A and check that B's outputs stay fixed. This simple perturbation test can expose a missing segment mask. Also inspect shifted labels after packing, because attention isolation and target alignment guard different paths.

title: Test the exact template and training path

beats.say: The conversation's behavior depends on its complete serialization. The template defines role and ending boundaries, tokenization fixes their IDs, the shift defines next-token pairs, and the loss mask chooses supervised targets. Packing adds attention and target-boundary checks.

Before fine-tuning, print a collated multi-turn example with token IDs, roles, labels, validity, and segment IDs aligned in one view. Compare a training sequence with the exact generation prefix used at serving. Those concrete tensors reveal where the contract changed.

title: An input repair precedes the quality comparison

beats.say: The training manifest binds checkpoint, tokenizer revision, resolved template and whether special tokens are added after rendering. The matching article candidate proceeds to evaluation. The drifted candidate changes the template family and enables a second special-token pass; both differences block it before a model-quality decision.

Diagnose a new user turn by inspecting the response cue when the checkpoint needs one. Diagnose doubled beginning or ending tokens by counting IDs after the real path. For a long-thread failure inspect retained policy evidence. For a correct answer followed by rambling compare the engine’s stop IDs with the template’s intended ending.

When a hosted endpoint hides the tokenizer, compare what you sent. Check the messages, tools and controls against the request schema, then compare the reported token counts. Once the inputs match, use the same decoding settings on held-out questions and score each checkpoint’s answers against the supplied evidence.

title: Validate metric types before comparing the thresholds

beats.say: The article’s sample gate checks one hundred cases per candidate. Both candidates match the training template. The gate requires at least ninety-eight percent grounded answers, zero critical errors and p ninety-five latency of at most seven hundred milliseconds. Candidate A reports ninety-nine percent, zero errors and six hundred twenty milliseconds. Check each value against its threshold. A passes. It can proceed to case review.

Candidate B reports ninety-four percent grounded answers, one critical error and four hundred ten milliseconds. Does B clear the same gate? Compare all three measurements. Hold candidate B. Its grounded rate falls short, and its critical error alone would block it. Its lower latency meets only the speed requirement.

Check the raw values before comparing thresholds. In the article’s Python gate, the rate and latency must arrive as an int or a float, and the critical count must arrive as an int. The function checks the exact types, so a boolean fails even though Python allows it in arithmetic. Rates must be finite and between zero and one. Counts and latency must be nonnegative, and latency must be finite.
A NaN can evade ordinary threshold comparisons, so reject it before those comparisons. A string saying yes is not literal boolean true for template parity.

Candidate A moves on to review. Read the cases where its answer lacked support. Save the requests and scores together so a reviewer can trace each miss to the evidence. Use those cases to choose what to monitor after release.

title: Audit a fresh reply

beats.say: Try a fresh toy row. The user asks, Ready? The assistant says Yes and ends its turn. The last slot is padding. Read the bottom row under each predictor.
Its label should be the ID of the next selected token, or minus one hundred if that prediction is skipped. One cell is wrong. Which predictor needs a different label, and which ID belongs there?

Put nineteen under position two. That assistant header predicts Yes. One step later, Yes predicts the real ending. Both the ending and the pad have ID twenty-three. Only the ending has a valid position inside the reply, so keep the padding prediction ignored.

Before serving this conversation with its full history, count the space it needs. The serialized prompt takes nine hundred seventy tokens. Reserve ninety-six for the reply. The limit is one thousand twenty-four, with no other overhead. We are forty-two tokens over.

One old exchange uses forty-five tokens and contains none of the required policy evidence. Remove that whole exchange. Nine hundred twenty-five plus ninety-six gives one thousand twenty-one. We have three slots to spare.
Back to the training row. Extend the answer by one word, indeed. The same ending and the same pad move over together. Which position now predicts the real ending?

Position four, the word indeed. Its next label is twenty-three. Position five already contains that ending. What follows it is padding, so its prediction is skipped. That is how to check whether a row actually teaches the handoff.

Now serve that same reply. The decoder has just produced the trained ending, twenty-three, and it still has room to generate. This toy server stops only when the latest ID belongs to its stop set. The set contains forty-two. Does this token stop the decoder?

The decoder asks for another token. The emitted ID passed forty-two without a match. Add twenty-three to the stop set. Replay the same emission. This time it stops. Training gave the last answer word a target of twenty-three. Serving returned the answer because the emitted ID matched the configured set.
